narrative: During the 1950s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and identity. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth of kinky hair, was likely worn by some individuals during this time period, although specific documentation from the era is limited. Cornrows, a traditional style of three-strand braids originating from African cultures, may have also been popular among Black and African women. Protective hairstyles, which minimize manipulation and exposure to environmental elements, would have been essential for preserving Afro-textured hair health during this time. Unfortunately, there is no specific information available about the 1950s regarding dreadlocks, locs, Bantu knots, box braids, or Jheri curls, indicating that these styles may not have been as prominent or widely adopted during this era. Nevertheless, it is clear that Black and African women's hair culture was rich in tradition and identity, reflecting their connection to African heritage and community.
